content_voiceover: Memorize this table cold, it's classic boards material. Hereditary hemochromatosis has four types by gene: type 1 is HFE, the most common by far; type 2a is HJV, hemojuvelin, causing juvenile hemochromatosis with severe early-onset disease; type 2b is HAMP, which encodes hepcidin itself, also a juvenile form; type 3 is TfR2; and type 4 is ferroportin-1, which behaves differently from the others, autosomal dominant with a tendency toward reticuloendothelial iron loading. Mechanistically, HFE protein is expressed in duodenal crypt cells and reticuloendothelial cells, binds beta-2-microglobulin, and modulates transferrin receptor-1 affinity — it's part of the iron-sensing complex that ultimately drives hepcidin expression, so HFE mutation means inappropriately low hepcidin and unchecked iron absorption. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and C282Y homozygosity is the classic genotype, accounting for the large majority of clinically significant cases; H63D is a weaker, lower-penetrance variant. The classic vignette is a middle-aged man with weakness, weight loss, arthralgias, loss of libido or impotence, bronze or gray skin pigmentation, hepatomegaly, abnormal liver function progressing to cirrhosis, diabetes — the classic bronze diabetes — and cardiac complaints. Workup starts with transferrin saturation and ferritin, liver biopsy if ferritin exceeds 800, and genetic testing to confirm. Treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy, started when ferritin is over 300, targeting hematocrit 34 to 36 and eventually maintenance ferritin 20 to 30.
keypoints: Type 1 HFE, Type 2a HJV, Type 2b HAMP (hepcidin), Type 3 TfR2, Type 4 ferroportin
